newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan disappointed by India's Kashmir position.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan disappointed by India's Kashmir position.

text.p: Pakistan said on Thursday it was "a little disappointed" by an Indian statement that re-staked New Delhi's claim over divided Kashmir soon after the latest peace talks between the two old foes.
However, a Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman said he did not expect future talks to be hit by Indian Foreign Ministry secretary Salman Haider's remarks on Wednesday.
Haider said that India wanted to focus on Pakistani military "occupation" of part of the region.
Asked if Islamabad was disappointed by Haider's remarks in New Delhi, the spokesman said: "Well we are a little disappointed."

Haider also said New Delhi expected the talks over Kashmir to focus on Pakistan's support for militancy in the Indian-ruled part of the region and not on the legitimacy of Indian rule, which is questioned by Islamabad.

The diplomat, who led the Indian delegation at a round of talks in Islamabad that ended on Monday, denied India had made a landmark concession by agreeing to put Kashmir on the agenda for future talks, although Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif had called it a "major breakthrough" in relations between the two countries.
The Pakistani spokesman called Haider's remarks propaganda, but acknowledged that it was not hostile propaganda, which the two sides had agreed in the talks to avoid.

"We would, however, wish to reiterate that (the) internationally recognised position is that Jammu and Kashmir is a disputed territory, the future status of which is to be determined through a reference to the people in terms of the United Nations Security Council resolutions."

Both Pakistan and India claim the right to rule over Jammu and Kashmir, which has sparked two of the three wars between the two countries since their independence from Britain in 1947. India rules two-thirds of Kashmir and Pakistan the rest.

"This is the first time that the two countries have agreed to formally list the oustanding issues and on a mechanism to address them," the Pakistani spokesman said. "This is a positive development which should be welcomed."

Haider, who is India's highest-ranking career diplomat, gave a sharply different version from that of Pakistan which analysts said underscored the deep split that continues between the South Asian nations nearly 50 years after they won independence.

"We have discussed Kashmir, in fact on a number of occasions, and we have also historically taken the position that we do not shy away from discussing Kashmir," Haider told a news conference after returning from Pakistan.
The Pakistani spokesman said that after the weekend's agreement on procedural issues, the proposed working groups would now go into susbtantive discussions.
"Any attempt at this stage to pre-judge or prejudice the eventual task of these working groups should be avoided," he said. "It would be counter-productive to conduct diplomacy through the media."

New Delhi regards all of Kashmir as an integral part of India, but Islamabad wants the predominantly Moslem Kashmiris to decide in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
Some of the Kashmiri groups fighting Indian rule since a rebellion erupted in 1990 seek to reunite Kashmir as an independent state.
